Ordering a coffee: your first real excha:
Everything in stage 2, used in the one transaction you will have most often. Learn this whole exchange as a unit.

**The coffees, because the names are not optional:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **ελληνικός καφές** | Greek coffee, boiled in a briki, grounds in the cup |
| **σκέτος** | without sugar |
| **μέτριος** | with a little sugar |
| **γλυκός** | sweet |
| **φραπέ** | instant coffee shaken cold with ice — the summer default |
| **φρέντο εσπρέσο** | cold espresso, shaken |
| **φρέντο καπουτσίνο** | the same with cold milk foam |
| **ζεστός** / **κρύος** | hot / cold |
| **με γάλα** / **χωρίς γάλα** | with / without milk |
| **για εδώ** / **για πάνω** | to drink here / to take away |

**The exchange:**

— **Καλημέρα!**
— **Καλημέρα. Τι θα πάρετε;** *(What will you have?)*
— **Έναν ελληνικό μέτριο, παρακαλώ.**
— **Κάτι άλλο;** *(Anything else?)*
— **Ένα κουλούρι. Πόσο κάνει;**
— **Δύο ευρώ και πενήντα.**
— **Ευχαριστώ.**
— **Παρακαλώ. Καλή σας μέρα!**

**What is in that, grammatically**, all of it from this stage: **έναν** is the masculine accusative of the indefinite article, because **καφές** is masculine and it is the object of an unspoken *I want*. **Μέτριο** agrees with it in gender and case. **Πόσο κάνει** is the price question. **Παρακαλώ** is doing its third job — *you are welcome*.

**Θα πάρετε** is a future, which is stage 6 — recognise it, do not analyse it.

**The short version, if the full one deserts you:** point and say **Αυτό, παρακαλώ.** Then **Ευχαριστώ.** That works everywhere and it is not rude.

**Other everyday orders**, built the same way:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Ένα νερό, παρακαλώ.** | A water, please. |
| **Μια μπύρα.** | A beer. |
| **Ένα τοστ.** | A toasted sandwich. |
| **Δύο σουβλάκια με πίτα.** | Two souvlaki in pita. |
| **Έναν φραπέ γλυκό με γάλα.** | A sweet frappé with milk. |
| **Τον λογαριασμό, παρακαλώ.** | The bill, please. |

**The social fact worth knowing.** Coffee in Greek life is an hour, not a drink — **πάμε για καφέ** is an invitation to sit down with someone, and it is how most friendships in a parish are actually conducted. Being able to accept it, and to order once you are there, is a more useful piece of Greek than any amount of grammar.

**Practice.** Read the exchange aloud, both parts, five times. Then order five different things out loud. Then say **Πάμε για καφέ;** — and be ready for a yes.
Shadowing, and how to do it:
The single most effective speaking exercise available without another person, and ten minutes of it a day is worth more than an hour of silent study.

**What it is.** You play a short piece of Greek audio and speak along with it, at the same time, matching the speed, the rhythm and the intonation as closely as you can. Not repeating after — speaking **with**.

**Why it works.** Three things improve at once: the mouth learns to make Greek sequences at Greek speed, the ear learns the rhythm, and the chunks of language go in as wholes rather than as assembled words. It is also the only exercise that makes you speak faster than your grammar can keep up with, which is the point.

**The method:**

1. **Pick ten to twenty seconds of audio** you understand completely. Understanding first, shadowing second.
2. **Listen twice** without speaking.
3. **Read the text while listening**, if you have it.
4. **Speak along, with the text**, several times.
5. **Speak along without the text.**
6. **Then speak it alone**, from memory, at the same speed.

**Ten minutes, on the same ten seconds, is correct.** The exercise is repetition of a tiny piece, not coverage.

**What to shadow at this stage:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Pimsleur** | already built this way — answer out loud, do not skip the speaking prompts |
| **Language Transfer** | pause and say every answer aloud before the student on the recording does |
| **Super Easy Greek** | short, subtitled, and at a real speed |
| **The lesson examples here** | read aloud, then shadow the Forvo recording of the same word |
| **A Greek song** | genuinely useful, and the lyrics are on stixoi.info |

**What to listen for in your own voice:**

- **The stress on the right syllable** — the thing Greek marks and you are learning to hear.
- **Full vowels**, with no English mumble in the unstressed ones.
- **One tap on the ρ.**
- **The rhythm of the whole phrase** rather than the correctness of each word.

**The embarrassment is the exercise.** Shadowing feels ridiculous, especially the first week, and it is the reason most learners never do it — which is also why it works so well for the ones who do. Nobody is listening.

**Where it pays off.** The gap between knowing a phrase and being able to say it at speed is the gap that keeps people silent at church. Shadowing closes exactly that gap, and nothing else does.

**Practice.** Take ten seconds of Super Easy Greek, or one Pimsleur exchange. Do the six steps on it, for ten minutes. Then do the same ten seconds again tomorrow.
Writing, from the first week:
Three sentences a day, by hand, in Greek letters. It is a small habit and it does several things nothing else does.

**Why write at all**, when the goal is talking to people:

1. **It forces the endings.** Speaking lets you mumble past a case ending; writing does not.
2. **It makes the spelling a question.** Which *i*? Which *o*? That is the Spelling track's subject and writing is where it gets tested.
3. **It makes the grammar explicit.** A sentence you can write is a sentence you understand; one you can only say may be a memorised chunk.
4. **It is the slowest and most deliberate form of practice**, which is why it catches what the others miss.

**The habit: three sentences a day, by hand.** About yourself, about the day, about what you did and what you want. Not translations of English — sentences you compose in Greek with the grammar you have.

**Starting material**, from this stage alone:

- **Είμαι ο [name]. Είμαι από την Αγγλία. Μένω στο York.**
- **Σήμερα πάω στην εκκλησία.**
- **Έχω δύο παιδιά. Τα παιδιά μου είναι μικρά.**
- **Μου αρέσει ο ελληνικός καφές.**
- **Δεν ξέρω πολλά ελληνικά, αλλά μαθαίνω.**

**That last sentence is worth memorising** as a sentence: *I do not know much Greek, but I am learning.* It is the single most useful thing to be able to say for the next year, and people answer it warmly.

**Then correct yourself.** Write the three sentences, then go back over them asking three questions: is every noun's gender right, is every ending right, is every accent there. That self-check is most of the value.

**Where to get corrections.** The dictionary at greek-language.gr for the inflection tables; Lexiscope for any form you are unsure of; and the deck, which will tell you which spelling a word takes. There is no teacher in this curriculum, so checking is a habit rather than a service.

**Keep them.** A notebook or a file, dated. In three months the first page becomes the clearest evidence of progress you will have, and that matters more than it sounds in a long route.

**Typing counts for some of it**, since you set the keyboard up in stage 1 — but handwriting at least some of it is better, for the reason stage 1's handwriting lesson gave.

**Practice.** Write three sentences now, by hand, about today. Then check each one for gender, endings and accents. Then do the same tomorrow.
Reading: the school readers:
What to read at the end of stage 2, which is written for Greek six-year-olds and is therefore exactly right.

**ebooks.edu.gr is the whole resource** — every Greek state school textbook, free, in PDF and in a browser reader. The ones you want:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Γλώσσα Α΄ Δημοτικού** | Language, first year of primary. Short sentences, present tense, enormous illustrations. |
| **Ανθολόγιο Α΄–Β΄ Δημοτικού** | the reader — stories, poems and rhymes for the first two years |
| **Γλώσσα Β΄ Δημοτικού** | the second year, which is the right target by the end of stage 3 |

**Why children's school material rather than a graded reader for foreigners.** It is free, there is a mountain of it, it is written by people whose job is teaching reading, and it is real Greek rather than constructed Greek. The vocabulary is a child's, which means it is concrete and high-frequency — exactly the words you want first.

**The one drawback**, and it is worth knowing: it assumes a child who already speaks Greek, so the grammar is not graded the way a textbook for foreigners would grade it. You will meet a past tense in week one. Read past it.

**How to read at this level:**

1. **Read aloud.** Always, at this stage. Reading Greek silently this early builds a reader and not a speaker.
2. **Do not look everything up.** One or two words a page, the ones that block the sentence.
3. **Reread.** The same page three times is better than three pages once.
4. **Stop when it stops being comprehensible**, and go back a level.

**The other free reading at this level:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The church notice board** | short, repetitive, weekly, and the vocabulary you most want |
| **Signs and labels**, from stage 1 | still working |
| **Children's books**, if anyone in the parish has any to lend | |
| **Greek Wikipedia's simple articles** | harder than they look; keep for stage 3 |
| **Song lyrics on stixoi.info** | with the song playing |

**What not to read yet:** newspapers, Greek Wikipedia proper, anything from the Church beyond the notice board. All of them are stage 8 and beyond, and attempting them now produces a page of dictionary lookups and no reading.

**The target for the end of stage 2** is a page of **Γλώσσα Α΄ Δημοτικού** read aloud, understood, without stopping more than once or twice.

**Practice.** Download **Γλώσσα Α΄ Δημοτικού** today. Read its first two pages aloud. Note how many words blocked you — then read the same pages again tomorrow and notice the number drop.
Review: stage 2:
The end of stage 2, which is the A1 level. What should be true, and what stage 3 does.

**What should now be true:**

- **είμαι** and **έχω**, all six persons, cold.
- The three genders, and the habit of learning every noun with its article.
- The definite article in all four nominative and accusative forms, said without thinking.
- **ένας / μία / ένα**, and **έναν** before a masculine object.
- Nominative against accusative: what each is for, and that prepositions take the accusative.
- The noun patterns: masculine **-ος, -ας, -ης**; feminine **-α, -η** and the **-ση** plurals in **-εις**; neuter **-ο, -ι, -μα**.
- Verbs in **-ω**, and the second class in **-άω/-ώ** and **-ώ/-είς**, with the stress telling you which.
- **δεν** for statements, **μην** for commands, and the double negative being correct.
- Questions by intonation alone, and the eight question words — with **πού/που** and **πώς/πως** distinguished by the accent.
- Adjectives agreeing in gender, number and case, and the adverb being the neuter plural.
- The strong pronouns, used only for emphasis.
- **αυτός** and **εκείνος**, with the article kept: **αυτό το παιδί**.
- **υπάρχει** and **υπάρχουν** for *there is*, and **έχει** in speech.
- The possessives after the noun, with the second accent where it is needed.
- The weak object pronouns before the verb and after a command.
- **μου αρέσει** against **μου αρέσουν**, and the family of verbs like it.
- **σε, από, για, με**, and **στον / στη / στο** merged.
- The place words, and giving simple directions.
- **εσύ** against **εσείς**, and **Πάτερ** for the priest.
- Numbers to a thousand, prices, and the shop sentences.
- The time, the days, the months, the seasons, and nine feast-day greetings.
- The parish vocabulary: the building, the people, the services, and what people say.
- Ordering a coffee, start to finish.
- Three habits running: shadowing, three written sentences a day, and reading the school readers aloud.

**What stage 2 deliberately did not do.** No genitive, no past tense, no future, no subjunctive, and no aspect. Every verb has been in the present, and that is why everything so far has been about now.

**What stage 3 does.** The cases, properly: the genitive — *of*, possession, and a great deal else — the vocative, the full declension of adjectives and pronouns, comparatives, and the **Forms track** opening with all of it as reference tables. By the end of it the noun system is complete and you can say what belongs to whom.

**And the Spelling track should already be running.** If it is not, start Spelling 1 now: it pairs with this stage, and the endings you have just learned are exactly what it drills.

**Practice.** Go down the list. Then hold a two-minute conversation with yourself out loud, using only stage 2 grammar: who you are, where you are from, what you have, what you like, where you are going on Sunday.
What the Spelling track is for:
**Spelling track, module 1 of 5. Run this module alongside stage 2**, at about one of these lessons for every three or four route lessons.

**The problem, stated once more.** Greek is read in one direction and spelled in the other. Given the letters you can always say the word; given the sound you cannot always write it, because five vowel sounds share about a dozen spellings and which one a word takes is a historical fact.

**What this track does about it.** Three things, in order of how much they pay:

1. **The endings.** Most of the *i*, *e* and *o* decisions in any Greek sentence are in word endings, and endings are decided by **grammar**, not by history. **-ει** is a verb, **-η** is a feminine noun, **-οι** is a masculine plural. That is a rule, it covers most of the problem, and it is this module.
2. **The patterns in stems.** Not rules, but strong tendencies and recognisable families — the **-ση** nouns, the **ευ-** words, the doubled consonants.
3. **The word-by-word remainder**, which is the deck's job.

**Why drill rather than read.** You asked for drills and the subject deserves them: spelling is recall, not understanding. Reading about **ει** against **η** teaches you nothing you cannot already see; writing fifty words from dictation and checking them teaches you exactly where your gaps are.

**The drill, and it is the same every time:**

1. **Read a list of words aloud.**
2. **Cover them.**
3. **Write them from memory, by hand, with their accents.**
4. **Check, and mark only the wrong ones.**
5. **Rewrite the wrong ones three times each.**
6. **Do the same list again tomorrow**, then in three days, then in a week.

**Ten minutes, and only the words you got wrong.** A list you can already spell is wasted time.

**Where the words come from:** the deck, which carries a spelling card for any word whose *i* or *o* is not predictable, and the three sentences a day from stage 2, which is where your own errors appear.

**What the track covers, module by module:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Spelling 1** | the *i*, *e* and *o* spellings, the endings, final **-ν**, the accent rules, diaeresis and syllables |
| **Spelling 2** | the noun and adjective endings in full, including the genitive, and the **-ση / -ξη / -ψη** family |
| **Spelling 3** | the verb endings in every tense, the augment, and the perfective stems' spellings |
| **Spelling 4** | doubled consonants, the **ευ-** and **αυ-** families, prefixes, and compounds |
| **Spelling 5** | abbreviations, numerals, punctuation in full, capitalisation, and handwriting at speed |

**Practice.** Take ten words you have already learned — from the deck — and do the six-step drill on them now. Note which ones you got wrong. Those are the only ones that matter.
The i sounds: ι η υ ει οι:
Five spellings, one sound, and the first thing to do is separate what is decided by grammar from what has to be memorised.

**The sound is *i* in all of these**: **ι, η, υ, ει, οι** — and **υι**, which is rare enough to ignore.

**Where grammar decides, and it is most of them:**

| Ending | Spelling | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| verb, 3rd person singular | **-ει** | γράφει, θέλει, μπορεί |
| verb, 2nd person singular | **-εις** | γράφεις, θέλεις |
| feminine noun, singular | **-η** | η πόλη, η αδελφή, η αγάπη |
| feminine adjective, singular | **-η** | καλή, μεγάλη, ωραία — and η |
| masculine noun, nominative plural | **-οι** | οι δάσκαλοι, οι φίλοι |
| **-ση / -ξη / -ψη** noun, plural | **-εις** | οι πόλεις, οι τάξεις, οι σκέψεις |
| neuter noun, singular | **-ι** | το παιδί, το σπίτι, το κερί |
| diminutive | **-άκι** | το παιδάκι, το καφεδάκι |

**Learn that table as rules and the endings stop being guesswork.** It is the highest-value page in this track.

**Where the stem has to be memorised**, with the commonest examples in each spelling:

- **ι**: είμαι, πίνω, ίδιος, ιστορία, φίλος, πολιτική, κίνηση
- **η**: ήλιος, μήνας, ημέρα, κήπος, ζωή, νίκη, ψυχή
- **υ**: μύτη, ύψος, γυναίκα, κύριος, φύλλο, θυμάμαι, σύμφωνα
- **ει**: είναι, εικόνα, ειρήνη, κλειδί, παιδεία, θείος
- **οι**: οικογένεια, οικία, ποιος, κοιτάζω, κοινός, ανοίγω

**Two patterns worth having**, because they cover a lot of words at once:

1. **Words with a clear English cousin usually keep the ancient spelling**, and the English spelling preserves it. **Ψυχή** → *psychology*, so **υ**. **Ιστορία** → *history*, so **ι**. **Ειρήνη** → *Irene*, so **ει**. **Οικονομία** → *economy*, so **οι**. This is a genuinely reliable trick for the educated vocabulary, which is a large slice of Greek.
2. **The -ια / -εια endings on abstract nouns**: **οικογένεια, παιδεία, αλήθεια, ιστορία**. The **-εια** ones usually come from an adjective; the **-ια** ones from a noun. A tendency rather than a rule, and worth noticing.

**The accent does not help with the spelling** — it says where the stress is and nothing about which *i*.

**Practice.** Drill the eight-row grammar table until you can say which spelling each ending takes without looking. Then do the six-step drill on these twenty words: **πόλη, παιδί, φίλοι, γράφει, γράφεις, πόλεις, γυναίκα, εικόνα, οικογένεια, ήλιος, μύτη, ψυχή, είναι, κλειδί, μήνας, σπίτι, ιστορία, ειρήνη, καφεδάκι, τάξεις**.
The e sounds: ε and αι:
Two spellings, one sound, and this one is much smaller than the *i* problem — because **ε** is the default and **αι** is a short list.

**ε is the normal spelling.** If you have no reason to think otherwise, write **ε**.

**Where αι appears, and it is mostly grammar again:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **και** | and — the commonest word in the language |
| **ναι** | yes |
| **είναι** | is, are |
| **the mediopassive verb endings** | **-μαι, -σαι, -ται, -νται** — είμαι, κάθομαι, γράφεται |
| **a set of stems** | παιδί, γυναίκα, αίμα, αίθουσα, καινούργιος, παίζω, παίρνω, φαίνομαι, χαίρομαι, λαιμός, ναύτης? no — ναι-words only |

**The mediopassive endings are the big grammatical case.** Every verb in the middle or passive voice — **είμαι, έρχομαι, κάθομαι, θυμάμαι, φαίνομαι, χαίρομαι** — ends in **-μαι** and never **-με**. That is stage 4's grammar and this is its spelling: if a verb's *I* form ends in the *me* sound, it is **-μαι**.

**Against which, -με is the active first person plural**: **γράφουμε, θέλουμε, είμαστε**. So **-ουμε** with ε, and **-ομαι** with αι, and the two are never confused once you know which voice you are in.

**The plural endings are all ε**: **-ες** (οι γυναίκες, οι μαθητές), **-ετε** (γράφετε), **-ες** on adjectives (καλές).

**The stems have to be learned**, and the English-cousin trick works here too: **παιδί** → *paediatric*, so **αι**. **Αίμα** → *haemoglobin*, so **αι**. **Καινούργιος** → *Cenozoic*, **καινο-** meaning new. **Γυναίκα** → *gynaecology*. Four words, four English words that preserve the spelling.

**ε in stems, for contrast**: **μέρα, πέντε, δέκα, θέλω, ξέρω, μένω, φέρνω, έχω, λέω, νερό, μεγάλος**. All of them common, all of them plain **ε**.

**The one pair worth drilling as a pair**: **παιδιά** (children) and **πεδιά** (plains). Different words, different spellings, same sound — and the first is the one you will write.

**Practice.** Drill these twenty: **και, ναι, είναι, παιδί, γυναίκα, αίμα, παίζω, παίρνω, χαίρομαι, έρχομαι, μέρα, πέντε, θέλω, ξέρω, νερό, γράφουμε, γράφετε, καλές, μαθητές, μένω**. Then write the six mediopassive endings from memory.
The o sounds: ο and ω:
Two spellings, one sound, and this is the easiest of the three — because the grammar decides almost all of it.

**Where grammar decides:**

| Ending | Spelling | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| verb, 1st person singular | **-ω** | γράφω, θέλω, μπορώ, αγαπώ |
| neuter noun, singular | **-ο** | το βιβλίο, το δώρο, το πρόσωπο |
| masculine noun, nominative | **-ος** | ο δάσκαλος, ο φίλος |
| masculine noun, accusative | **-ο** | τον δάσκαλο, τον φίλο |
| adjective, neuter | **-ο** | καλό, μεγάλο |
| genitive plural | **-ων** | των παιδιών, των γυναικών |
| adverbs from adjectives | **-ως** sometimes | κυρίως, ακριβώς, τελείως |

**So: verbs take ω, nouns take ο.** That single sentence settles the overwhelming majority of cases, and it is worth saying out loud a few times because it is the most useful spelling rule in the language.

- **γράφω** — I write, with ω · **το γράψιμο** — the writing, with ο
- **θέλω** — I want · **το θέλημα** — the will

**The genitive plural -ων** is the other grammatical **ω**, and it is everywhere once stage 3 opens: **των ανθρώπων, των παιδιών, των πόλεων**.

**Where the stem has to be memorised:**

- **ω in stems**: ώρα, ωραίος, ζώο, φως, χώρα, σώμα, όνειρο? no — **ώ** words: ώρα, ωραίος, ώμος, ζώνη, χώρος, πρώτος, κώδικας, μεγάλωσα
- **ο in stems**: όνομα, όχι, πόλη, μόνο, κόσμος, δρόμος, λόγος, πρόσωπο, σπορ

**The English-cousin trick again**: **ώρα** → *hour*, from the same root; **ζώο** → *zoo*; **φως/φωτο-** → *photograph*; **χώρα** → no cousin; **πρώτος** → *prototype*; **κώδικας** → *code*. English's *o* and *oo* spellings do not map reliably, but the learned words — *photo-, proto-, zoo-, -tomy* — do preserve the ancient **ω** where it was there.

**The -ώνω verb family** is a useful cluster: **μεγαλώνω** (grow), **τελειώνω** (finish), **σηκώνω** (lift), **αρχίζω**? no. The **-ώνω** verbs all take ω in both syllables and there are dozens of them.

**One pair to drill**, because the words are common and the difference is only spelling: **μόνο** (only) and **μονό** (single) and **μόνος** (alone). Same for **καλό** (good, neuter) and **καλώ** (I call).

**Practice.** Say the rule aloud — verbs ω, nouns ο — five times. Then drill these twenty: **γράφω, θέλω, μπορώ, βιβλίο, δώρο, δάσκαλος, φίλο, καλό, ώρα, ωραίος, ζώο, φως, χώρα, όνομα, όχι, κόσμος, δρόμος, πρώτος, τελειώνω, των παιδιών**.
The endings, drilled:
The consolidation lesson of this module: every ending from stage 2 with its spelling, as one page to drill against.

**Nouns:**

| | Singular | Plural |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Masculine** | **-ος**, **-ας**, **-ης** → acc. **-ο**, **-α**, **-η** | **-οι**, **-ες**, **-ες** → acc. **-ους**, **-ες**, **-ες** |
| **Feminine** | **-α**, **-η** (unchanged in acc.) | **-ες**, or **-εις** for the **-ση/-ξη/-ψη** nouns |
| **Neuter** | **-ο**, **-ι**, **-μα** | **-α**, **-ια**, **-ματα** |

**Adjectives**: **-ος / -η / -ο**, plural **-οι / -ες / -α**, masculine accusative plural **-ους**.

**Verbs, present tense:**

| | Class A | Class B1 | Class B2 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| I | **-ω** | **-άω / -ώ** | **-ώ** |
| you | **-εις** | **-άς** | **-είς** |
| he/she/it | **-ει** | **-άει / -ά** | **-εί** |
| we | **-ουμε** | **-άμε / -ούμε** | **-ούμε** |
| you (pl.) | **-ετε** | **-άτε** | **-είτε** |
| they | **-ουν** | **-άνε / -ούν** | **-ούν** |

**The three rules that cover nearly all of it:**

1. **A verb's *I* ends in -ω. A noun's neuter singular ends in -ο.**
2. **-ει is a verb, -η is a feminine noun, -οι is a masculine plural, -ι is a neuter.**
3. **-ες is a plural, -αι is a mediopassive verb ending.**

**Now the drill, and this is the one to repeat weekly.** Here are twenty-four forms. Read them aloud, cover them, write them from memory with accents, check, and rewrite only the wrong ones:

**γράφω · γράφεις · γράφει · γράφουμε · γράφετε · γράφουν · μπορώ · μπορείς · μπορεί · μπορούμε · αγαπάω · αγαπάς · η πόλη · οι πόλεις · η αδελφή · οι αδελφές · ο δάσκαλος · οι δάσκαλοι · τους δασκάλους · το παιδί · τα παιδιά · το μάθημα · τα μαθήματα · είμαι**

**Then the harder version**: have the English in front of you and write the Greek. *I write · you write · he writes · we write · I can · you can · the city · the cities · the teacher · the teachers · the child · the children · the lesson · the lessons · I am.*

**Where your errors will cluster**, going by what English speakers get wrong: **-ουμε** written **-ουμαι**; **-ει** and **-η** swapped; **-οι** written **-ι** in masculine plurals; **-εις** forgotten in the **-ση** plurals; and the accent dropped from **γράφουμε**.

**Practice.** Do the twenty-four-form drill now, then the English-to-Greek version tomorrow. Keep the list; it is the weekly test for this whole module.
Final -ν: when to write it:
A small rule with a lot of traffic, because the words it applies to are among the commonest in the language.

**The words that may or may not keep a final -ν:**

- **τον** and **την** — the accusative singular articles
- **έναν** — the masculine accusative of *one, a*
- **δεν** — not · **μην** — do not
- **αυτήν**, **σαν**, **πριν** — and a few others

**The rule: keep the -ν before a vowel, and before κ, π, τ, μπ, ντ, γκ, τσ, τζ, ξ, ψ. Drop it before everything else** — that is, before β, γ, δ, ζ, θ, λ, μ, ν, ρ, σ, φ, χ.

| Keep it | Drop it |
| --- | --- |
| **τον άντρα** | **το δάσκαλο** |
| **την Κυριακή** | **τη μητέρα** |
| **τον πατέρα** | **τη Θεσσαλονίκη** |
| **την τάξη** | **τη γυναίκα** |
| **έναν καφέ** | **ένα βιβλίο** (neuter anyway) |
| **στην Αθήνα** | **στη Λάρισα** |

**Why the rule is shaped like that.** The kept **-ν** is the one you can hear: before those consonants it voices them — *τον πατέρα* comes out *tom-batéra*, *την Κυριακή* as *tiŋ-gyriakí*. Before the others it would be inaudible, so the spelling drops it.

**The masculine τον keeps its -ν much more often in practice**, because dropping it would make it identical to the neuter **το** and lose the gender. Many writers and the school grammar keep **τον** always for exactly that reason, and that is the safer habit.

**δεν and μην are usually written with the -ν always**, again to avoid confusion — **δε** also exists as an old word for *but*, and **μη** as a prefix. Keeping them full is standard practice and never wrong.

**So the practical version for you:**

1. **Always write δεν and μην.**
2. **Always write τον** for the masculine.
3. **Apply the rule to την and στην**, which is where it genuinely varies.
4. **Write έναν** before a vowel or those consonants, **ένα** otherwise.

**Where it matters most: στη and στην**, which you will write in every third sentence. **στην Αθήνα, στην εκκλησία, στην τάξη** — kept; **στη Θεσσαλονίκη, στη δουλειά, στη μητέρα** — dropped.

**What the genitive plural does**: **-ων** always keeps its **ν**, in every word, with no rule to apply — **των παιδιών, των ανθρώπων**.

**Practice.** Write these twelve with the right form of the article: *(the) άντρα, μητέρα, Κυριακή, δουλειά, τάξη, γυναίκα, πατέρα, φίλο, εκκλησία, Θεσσαλονίκη, καφέ, βιβλίο*. Then write five sentences with **στη / στην** and check each one against the rule.
The accent rules in full:
Everything about the written accent, in one place, as rules to apply rather than facts to recall.

**The basics, from stage 1:**

1. **Every word of two or more syllables takes exactly one accent.**
2. **It falls on one of the last three syllables** — the rule of limitation.
3. **Monosyllables take none**, with the exceptions below.
4. **All-capital text takes none.**

**The accented monosyllables**, and the list is short and closed:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **ή** | or — to distinguish it from **η**, the feminine article |
| **πού** | where? — against **που**, *that / who* |
| **πώς** | how? — against **πως**, *that* |

**And the disambiguating accent on weak pronouns.** When a weak pronoun follows a word stressed on its third-from-last syllable and could be read as a possessive, it takes an accent of its own:

- **Ο πατέρας μού είπε…** — my father **told me**… (*μού* is *to me*, not *my*)
- **Ο δάσκαλός μου** — **my** teacher (the noun takes the second accent instead)

**That is the second accent**, and the rule is the rule of limitation doing its work: adding a clitic pushes the original stress past the third syllable from the end, so a second accent appears within the limit.

- **το όνομα** → **το όνομά μου** · **ο δάσκαλος** → **ο δάσκαλός μου** · **δώσε μου το** → **δώσε μού το**

**Where the accent moves when a word inflects**, which is the part to drill:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **ο άνθρωπος** → **του ανθρώπου**, **τους ανθρώπους** | forward one, by the rule of limitation |
| **το μάθημα** → **του μαθήματος** | forward one |
| **η κυβέρνηση** → **οι κυβερνήσεις** | forward one |
| **ο φίλος** → **του φίλου**, **τους φίλους** | no movement — already inside the limit |

**On a digraph, the accent goes on the second letter**: **παίζω, είμαι, πού, μπορείς**.

**With a diaeresis, both marks appear** when the vowel needs separating and carries the stress: **πρωτεΐνη**, **Μαΐου**, **ταΐζω**.

**In compounds, the accent is on the second element**, usually, and the first loses its own: **πολύ + κατοικία** → **πολυκατοικία**.

**What the accent never does:** mark length, mark pitch, or distinguish anything other than stress. One mark, one job — which is why the monotonic system replaced the old three accents and two breathings in 1982.

**Practice.** Accent these ten words from memory, out loud and then written: *ανθρωπος, μαθημα, μαθηματος, δασκαλος, δασκαλου, κυβερνησεις, παιζω, ειμαι, πολυκατοικια, ονομα μου*. Then write five sentences containing a possessive and check the second accent in each.
Diaeresis, apostrophe and syllables:
Three small orthographic systems, each of which decides how a word is read, and all three are rule-based rather than memorised.

**The diaeresis — τα διαλυτικά — breaks a digraph.** Two dots over ι or υ say "read these two vowels separately":

- **παϊδάκια** — *pa-i-dákia*, lamb chops. Without the dots, **παιδάκια**, *little children*. Two different words.
- **προϊόν** — product · **γαϊδούρι** — donkey · **ευνοϊκός** — favourable

**When it is omitted — and this is the rule:** when the **first** of the two vowels carries the accent, the accent already breaks the pair, so no dots are needed.

- **Μάιος** — May · **νεράιδα** — fairy · **ρολόι** — watch · **πλάι** — beside

**When both marks appear**: when the ι or υ itself is stressed and still needs separating.

- **Μαΐου** — of May · **πρωτεΐνη** — protein · **ταΐζω** — I feed

**And it is unnecessary where there was no digraph to break**: **πρωί** (morning), **Μωυσής** (Moses), **διυλιστήριο** (refinery) — **ωι**, **ωυ** and **ιυ** are not digraphs, so nothing has to be said.

**In all capitals the dots stay**, because there are no accents to do the job: **ΠΑΪΔΑΚΙΑ**, **ΠΡΟΪΟΝ**.

**The apostrophe marks a dropped vowel** — elision — and it is everywhere in speech and writing both:

- **σ' αγαπώ** ← σε αγαπώ · **απ' την Αθήνα** ← από την Αθήνα · **μ' αρέσει** ← μου αρέσει
- **θα 'ρθω** ← θα έρθω · **να 'ναι** ← να είναι

**Which is why a word can be unfindable in a dictionary**: put the vowel back and look again.

**Syllables — ο συλλαβισμός — matter for two reasons**: hyphenating at the end of a line, and knowing which syllable the accent is on. The rules:

1. **One consonant between two vowels goes with the following vowel**: πα-τέ-ρας, μη-τέ-ρα.
2. **Two consonants between vowels go with the following vowel if a Greek word can begin with that pair**: έ-θνος, κρύ-βω, Α-φρι-κή. If not, they split: άν-θρω-πος, θάλασ-σα? — no: **θά-λασ-σα**, because *σσ* cannot begin a word.
3. **Three consonants go with the following vowel if the first two can begin a word**: αι-σχρός; otherwise the first stays behind: άν-θρω-πος.
4. **Digraphs are never split** — neither vowel pairs (αι, ει, οι, ου, αυ, ευ) nor consonant pairs (μπ, ντ, γκ, τσ, τζ).

**Counting syllables is what the accent rules need**, so this is not an idle skill: to know whether the stress is on the third from the end you have to divide the word, and digraphs count as one.

**Practice.** Add the diaeresis where it belongs: *παιδακια (chops), προιον, Μαιος, Μαιου, πρωτεινη, ρολοι*. Then expand these: **σ' αγαπώ, απ' το σπίτι, θα 'ρθω**. Then divide into syllables and say where the stress is: **άνθρωπος, θάλασσα, οικογένεια, μπορείτε, εκκλησία**.
